text:
No, almost certainly not. At six people, microservices trade a problem you probably don't have (scaling teams and deployments independently) for ones you will: distributed debugging, network failure modes, versioning between services, duplicated infra and CI, and a large share of your engineering time going to plumbing instead of product. A well-structured monolith is the right default at this size.

What would change that: a specific, measured bottleneck a monolith can't solve, such as one component with radically different scaling or hardware needs (video processing, ML inference), a hard isolation requirement (compliance, security boundary), or a team grown large enough that deploy contention and merge conflicts are the actual constraint. "It feels messy" or "it'll scale better someday" doesn't qualify.

If the pain is real, fix it inside the monolith first:
- Enforce module boundaries (Packwerk, engines, or clear namespaces) so coupling is visible and limited.
- Move slow or bursty work to background jobs (Sidekiq, Solid Queue).
- Scale horizontally and add read replicas and caching before splitting anything.
- Speed up CI and deploys, which are usually the real complaint.

Well-bounded modules also make a later extraction cheap, if one is ever justified, so you lose little by waiting.

If you tell me what's actually hurting (slow deploys, scaling, test time, team conflicts), I can say whether any of it needs a split.
